newsitem.title: USA: ATHLETICS-U.S. OFFICIALS SUSPEND MARY SLANEY.
newsitem.headline: ATHLETICS-U.S. OFFICIALS SUSPEND MARY SLANEY.

text.p: - U.S. athletics officials have suspended Mary Slaney, making her ineligible for the national championships that began on Wednesday, an athletics source said.
The source, knowledgeable about the case, said a USA Track and Field (USATF) board had suspended the U.S. women's distance star on Tuesday night.
USATF spokesman Pete Cava declined comment. "I cannot say anything about Mary Slaney's status," Cava said.
Slaney's husband, Richard, said the couple had not been notified "personally."
"If that's what they have not come to Indianapolis. Why should she? To do what?" Slaney said from the couple's home in Eugene, Oregon.
He would not comment on whether Slaney, the queen of American runners, would seek arbitration or a court order in the case. "There probably would not be enough time," he said.
The decision to suspend Slaney was based on a review by the U.S. board of her drug test at last summer's U.S. Olympic trials, the source said.

Slaney was found during the test to have a higher than acceptable ratio of testosterone to epitestosterone. Any ratio higher than 6-1 is considered suspicious by the IAAF and the athlete can be suspended.

Slaney has consistently denied taking any substance banned by the IAAF. But IAAF general secretary Istvan Gyulai on Tuesday said, "There is a very clear indication that this (Slaney) is a doping case."
The IAAF almost two weeks ago suspended Slaney and fellow Americans Sandra Farmer-Patrick and Stephon Flenoy pending the outcome of their U.S. hearings

The international governing body on Tuesday followed up the suspension by sending official notification to U.S. officials. In the fax, the IAAF said Slaney was suspended and was ineligible to compete in the United States and internationally. It also said that other athletes could be suspended if they competed against Slaney.

The latter stipulation had concerned the 38-year-old Slaney and her husband, who said on Tuesday night that Mary Slaney would not come to the national championships if the IAAF threatened to ban other athletes.
A source said Slaney would be eligible for two more hearings before U.S. athletics panels if she wanted to pursue the suspension.

Cava, the USATF spokesman, said on Wednesday that when an athlete's doping test is found to be positive, the date of ineligibity begins with the day the sample was taken and all performances since that date would be invalid.

That means Slaney, if the disputed test is ultimately labeled positive, would be stripped of her silver medal performance in the women's 1,500 meters at the world indoor championships in March and she would be required to return $20,000 in prize money from the championships.
